\chapter{Asking Without a Question Word}
\label{ch:hi-polar-question}
\hlchaptermodality{74}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can turn any statement I own into a yes-or-no question with a fronted kya, ask the same question with the voice alone, and check a fact with the naa tag.}

Complete HI-R74-ask and run every joining word in the book once, then both question shapes: the one that does not know the answer and the one that expects agreement.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kyā …?]{\hi{क्या} …? — the yes-or-no question}

\label{lesson:HI-C74-kya-polar}



\begin{quote}
Retrieve the two items before this one by name: \textbf{-\hi{कर}} and \textbf{\hi{जब} … \hi{तब}}. Then say \textbf{\hi{हाँ}} and \textbf{\hi{नहीं}} — two answers with no question.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \hi{क्या} at the FRONT means nothing}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{क्या} \hi{आप} \hi{कल} \hi{आ} \hi{सकते} \hi{हैं}?} — \emph{kyā āp kal ā sakte haiṁ?} — \textbf{Can you come tomorrow?}
\end{quote}

Put \textbf{\hi{क्या}} at the very front and it stops meaning \emph{what}: it marks the sentence as a yes-or-no question and nothing else moves, because Hindi cannot invert the way English does with \emph{can you}.

Position is the whole difference:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{आप} \hi{क्या} \hi{कर} \hi{सकते} \hi{हैं}?} — \emph{what can you do?} — inside
  \item \textbf{\hi{क्या} \hi{आप} \hi{आ} \hi{सकते} \hi{हैं}?} — \emph{can you come?} — in front
\end{itemize}

Answer either with \textbf{\hi{हाँ}} or \textbf{\hi{नहीं}}. A language that cannot invert reaches for a particle; Persian and Russian do the same.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kyā āp kal ā sakte haiṁ?} and answer — \emph{hāṁ} or \emph{nahīṁ}
  \item the pair — \emph{āp kyā kar sakte haiṁ?} / \emph{kyā āp ā sakte haiṁ?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\hi{क्या}} mean at the very front? (\textbf{Nothing — it marks a yes-or-no question}.) What else moves? (\textbf{Nothing}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A5\%8D\%E0\%A4\%AF\%E0\%A4\%BE}{Wiktionary: \hi{क्या}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[āp ā sakte haiṁ?]{The question that is only a voice}

\label{lesson:HI-C74-question-rise}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\hi{क्या} \hi{आप} \hi{आ} \hi{सकते} \hi{हैं}?} — the question you got one lesson ago. Now say it again and leave the first word out.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{आप} \hi{आ} \hi{सकते} \hi{हैं}?} — \emph{āp ā sakte haiṁ?} — \textbf{Can you come?}
\end{quote}

Word for word that is a statement. What makes it a question is the \textbf{pitch of the last two syllables going up}, and nothing else. Speakers drop \textbf{\hi{क्या}} far more often than they use it, so this is the ordinary form and the particle is the careful one.

Say the pair and listen, do not read:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{आप} \hi{आ} \hi{सकते} \hi{हैं}.} — flat at the end — \emph{you can come}
  \item \textbf{\hi{आप} \hi{आ} \hi{सकते} \hi{हैं}?} — rising at the end — \emph{can you come?}
\end{itemize}

Two things follow. First, you can ask any yes-or-no question in Hindi today without learning another word — every statement in this book is already a question if you lift the end of it. Second, and less comfortable: a listening paper will hand you the rise \textbf{without} the particle, so the ear has to catch it. A candidate reading only for \textbf{\hi{क्या}} will hear a statement and answer nothing.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{āp ā sakte haiṁ.} flat, then \emph{āp ā sakte haiṁ?} rising
  \item the same sentence with the particle — \emph{kyā āp ā sakte haiṁ?}
  \item which of the three a Hindi speaker uses most — \textbf{the rise}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What turns \textbf{\hi{आप} \hi{आ} \hi{सकते} \hi{हैं}} into a question with no extra word? (\textbf{The pitch rising at the end}.) Which form do speakers use more often, that or \textbf{\hi{क्या}}? (\textbf{The rise}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[… hai nā?]{… \hi{है} \hi{ना}? — \textquotedblleft{}isn't it?\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:HI-C74-na-tag}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{क्या}} at the front asks something you do not know. Often you DO know, and want it confirmed. Different move, different word, other end.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: hanging a check on the end}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{चाय} \hi{ठीक} \hi{है} \hi{ना}?} — \emph{chāy ṭhīk hai nā?} — \textbf{The tea is fine, isn't it?}
\end{quote}

Take any statement you can make, put \textbf{\hi{ना}} on the end, and it becomes a check: you say what you believe and invite the listener to agree. The answer comes back as \textbf{\hi{हाँ}} or \textbf{\hi{नहीं}}.

Set the two questions side by side:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{क्या} \hi{चाय} \hi{ठीक} \hi{है}?} — \emph{is the tea fine?} — I do not know
  \item \textbf{\hi{चाय} \hi{ठीक} \hi{है} \hi{ना}?} — \emph{the tea is fine, isn't it?} — I think so; agree with me
\end{itemize}

Use the tag when you mean the particle and you have claimed to know the answer already.

One syllable buys a whole conversational turn: every sentence in this book is now something you can offer for agreement. The tag is the old negative \textbf{\hi{न}} used as an invitation — a negative asking for a \emph{yes}, exactly as English does in \emph{isn't it?} and Marathi with the same syllable.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{chāy ṭhīk hai nā?} then answer yourself — \emph{hāṁ}
  \item the pair — \emph{kyā chāy ṭhīk hai?} / \emph{chāy ṭhīk hai nā?}
  \item which one already believes the answer — \textbf{the tag}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\hi{ना}} on the end of a statement do? (\textbf{Asks the listener to confirm it}.) How is that different from \textbf{\hi{क्या}} at the front? (\textbf{\hi{क्या} does not know the answer; \hi{ना} expects agreement}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%A8\%E0\%A4\%BE}{Wiktionary: \hi{ना}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kyā …? · … nā? · … aur … · … kyoṁki …]{Everything that joins, and everything that asks}

\label{lesson:HI-R74-ask}



\begin{quote}
Seven chapters ago you could name a thousand Hindi things and say nothing about two of them at once. Name the three joiners this run opened with, and say where the verb of each half goes.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn — clauses underneath}
Say each of the four, and after each one name what the underneath clause is doing: a content, a reason, a time, a sequence.

\subsection*{Your turn — the two questions}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kyā āp kal ā sakte haiṁ?} — you do not know
  \item \emph{chāy ṭhīk hai nā?} — you think you do
  \item \emph{āp kab ā sakte haiṁ?} · \emph{āp kyoṁ nahīṁ ā sakte?}
  \item \emph{āp kal ā sakte haiṁ?} with no particle at all, on a rising voice
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which joining words treat the two halves as EQUALS? (\emph{\textbf{aur\emph{, \textbf{\hi{या}}, \textbf{\hi{लेकिन}}.) Which ones put one half UNDERNEATH the other? (\textbf{\hi{कि}}, \textbf{\hi{क्योंकि}}, \textbf{\hi{जब} … \hi{तब}}, \textbf{-\hi{कर}}.) And which single word means }what\emph{ in the middle of a sentence and nothing at all at the front? (\textbf{\hi{क्या}}.) Then stop.}}}
\end{tcolorbox}
